elements.name: Data Binding
elements.what: Declaratively connects a UI element's displayed value to a data source so changes propagate automatically instead of via hand-written synchronization code.
elements.problem: Keeping view and model state consistent by hand is repetitive and error-prone; binding centralizes the sync and lets direction (one-way source-to-view vs two-way round-trip) be declared, not coded.
elements.named_in: Data Binding Overview - WPF documentation - Microsoft

elements.name: Virtual DOM
elements.what: Keeps a lightweight in-memory tree describing the desired UI, diffs it against the previous tree on every update, and applies only the minimal set of mutations (reconciliation) to the real, expensive display tree.
elements.problem: Direct manipulation of a retained display tree (the browser DOM) is slow and hard to reason about; declaring the whole UI and diffing lets code be written as 'render from state' while paying only for what changed. Keyed list reconciliation and the incremental-DOM alternative are variants folded here.
elements.named_in: Reconciliation - React documentation - Meta

elements.name: Signals (fine-grained reactivity)
elements.what: State cells that automatically track which computations read them and re-run exactly those computations (computeds/effects) when the cell changes, giving fine-grained dependency-graph updates without diffing.
elements.problem: Coarse re-render-and-diff wastes work and manual subscription management leaks or over-fires; automatic dependency tracking updates precisely the affected derived values and effects. TC39 has a standard proposal based on Solid, Vue, Angular, MobX et al.
elements.named_in: JavaScript Signals standard proposal - TC39 (proposal-signals)

elements.name: Observable Streams
elements.what: An asynchronous push-based sequence abstraction: a producer pushes multiple values over time to subscribers, composable with declarative operators; the Reactive Streams specification adds demand-signalled flow control (backpressure).
elements.problem: Callback-based async event handling tangles composition, completion, and error propagation; observables extend the Observer pattern to sequences with uniform error/completion semantics, and backpressure keeps fast producers from overwhelming slow consumers (resilience-axis overlap noted).
elements.named_in: ReactiveX documentation - Introduction/Observable (reactivex.io)

elements.name: Event Delegation
elements.what: Attaches a single event handler on a common ancestor and uses event bubbling plus target inspection to handle events for many (possibly dynamically created) descendant elements.
elements.problem: Registering one handler per element wastes memory and breaks for elements added after registration; one delegated handler on the ancestor covers all current and future descendants.
elements.named_in: Event delegation - javascript.info (The Modern JavaScript Tutorial)

elements.name: Immediate-Mode GUI
elements.what: A GUI API style where user code re-declares the widgets to draw every frame inside the input/render loop (DoButton() each frame rather than CreateButton() once), with the library retaining little or no widget object state.
elements.problem: Retained widget trees force state duplication between application data and widget objects and constant synchronization; immediate mode derives the UI from application state each frame, eliminating the sync problem at the cost of per-frame re-specification. Coined by Casey Muratori (2002); Dear ImGui and Nuklear are canonical implementations.
elements.named_in: Immediate mode (computer graphics) - Wikipedia; Immediate-Mode Graphical User Interfaces - Casey Muratori (2005)
elements.borderline: API/state paradigm rather than a single mechanism, but named, recurring, and implementable inside one component - IN per altitude test.

elements.name: Retained-Mode GUI
elements.what: A GUI/graphics API style where the library retains a persistent object model of the scene (widget tree/scene graph) that client code creates once and mutates, with the library handling redraws from the retained model.
elements.problem: Re-specifying the whole UI every frame is wasteful for mostly-static interfaces; retaining the scene lets the library optimize redraw, hit-testing, and accessibility, at the cost of keeping the retained model in sync with application state. Historically the dominant GUI style.
elements.named_in: Retained mode - Wikipedia
elements.borderline: The dominant default paradigm; cataloged for contrast with immediate mode - arguably ambient rather than a reached-for element.

elements.name: Dirty Rectangles
elements.what: Tracks the screen regions invalidated since the last frame and redraws/blits only those rectangles instead of the whole display surface.
elements.problem: Full-screen redraw every frame wastes fill-rate when most of the display is unchanged; accumulating damage regions bounds redraw cost to what actually changed. A screen-space specialization of the dirty flag; games scout overlaps by design.
elements.named_in: Graphics Programming Black Book - Michael Abrash (1997)

elements.name: Event Loop
elements.what: A loop that continually waits for events/messages on a queue and dispatches each to its handler; the UI-heritage aliases message pump/message loop (Win32) and run loop (Apple) name the same mechanism.
elements.problem: A program must service many asynchronous input sources (user input, timers, I/O) on one thread without polling each; a single dispatch loop serializes handling and keeps the UI thread responsive. Carried here chiefly for the message-pump aka; the concurrency scout owns the primary entry.
elements.named_in: Event loop - Wikipedia

elements.name: Undo/Redo Command Stack
elements.what: Records executed operations as command objects (with state backups or inverse operations) on a history stack, so popping replays/reverts them to implement undo and redo.
elements.problem: Reversing arbitrary user operations requires either remembering prior state or an inverse for every action; reifying operations as stacked command objects makes multi-level undo/redo systematic.
elements.named_in: Command - Refactoring.Guru (command history / undo section)
elements.borderline: Composition of GoF Command + Memento rather than a primitive; included because it is independently named (command history) and recurring - decision logged.

elements.name: Reactive Programming
elements.what: A programming model in which programs are expressed as dataflows of time-varying values and the runtime automatically propagates changes through the dependency graph, as in a spreadsheet.
elements.problem: Interactive programs are dominated by manually wiring 'when X changes, update Y' logic (callback hell, inconsistent intermediate states); declaring dependencies and letting the system propagate changes removes that class of code. Umbrella over FRP, Rx, and signals.
elements.named_in: A Survey on Reactive Programming - Bainomugisha, Carreton, Van Cutsem, Mostinckx, De Meuter (ACM Computing Surveys, 2013)
elements.borderline: Umbrella programming model rather than a single mechanism; included per the asynchronous-programming-models precedent in the mission's anchor table - decision logged.

elements.name: Functional Reactive Programming
elements.what: Models interactive systems as compositions of first-class time-varying values (behaviors, denotationally continuous) and discrete event streams, manipulated with pure functional combinators.
elements.problem: Imperative event handling scatters temporal logic across callbacks and mutable state; FRP gives a denotational, composable semantics for time-varying computation. Distinct from the looser 'reactive programming' umbrella - FRP is the original, precisely-specified formulation.
elements.named_in: Functional Reactive Animation - Conal Elliott, Paul Hudak (ICFP 1997)

elements.name: Dirty Checking
elements.what: Detects state changes by re-evaluating watched expressions and comparing new values against stored previous values in a check loop (repeated until stable), rather than by intercepting writes.
elements.problem: When state can be mutated by arbitrary plain code, there is no write hook to observe; periodic compare-against-last-value detects any change at the cost of scanning all watchers per cycle. Canonical in AngularJS's $digest; contrast with signals' write-time tracking.
elements.named_in: AngularJS Developer Guide - Scopes ($digest / dirty checking)

elements.name: List Virtualization
elements.what: Renders only the subset of a long scrollable list that is visible in the viewport (plus a small buffer), creating, recycling, and repositioning a fixed pool of item views as the user scrolls.
elements.problem: Instantiating a widget per item makes large lists consume unbounded memory and layout time; virtualizing bounds live widget count to the viewport size. Named across stacks: WPF UI virtualization, Android RecyclerView view recycling, react-window windowing, CDK virtual scrolling.
elements.named_in: Optimizing Performance: Controls (UI Virtualization) - WPF documentation - Microsoft

elements.name: Optimistic UI Update
elements.what: Applies the expected result of a user action to local UI state immediately, before server confirmation, then reconciles with the authoritative response - rolling back if the operation fails.
elements.problem: Waiting a network round-trip for every mutation makes interfaces feel sluggish; predicting the result hides latency, at the cost of needing rollback/reconciliation logic for the failure case.
elements.named_in: Apollo Client documentation - Optimistic mutation results

elements.name: Debounce
elements.what: Delays invoking a handler until a specified quiet period has elapsed since the last triggering event, collapsing a burst of events into a single trailing (or leading) invocation.
elements.problem: High-frequency event sources (keystrokes, resize, contact bounce in hardware switches) would trigger expensive work per event; debouncing runs the work once per burst. Scheduling scout overlaps by design; the term originates in switch debouncing (embedded).
elements.named_in: Underscore.js documentation - _.debounce

elements.name: Throttle
elements.what: Guarantees a handler runs at most once per fixed time window during a stream of events, dropping or deferring intermediate invocations.
elements.problem: Continuous event streams (scroll, mousemove, sensor polls) need regular but bounded processing; throttling caps invocation rate while still sampling the stream, unlike debounce which waits for silence. Scheduling scout overlaps by design.
elements.named_in: Underscore.js documentation - _.throttle

elements.name: Event Coalescing
elements.what: Merges multiple fine-grained input events that occur within one processing frame into a single delivered event, optionally exposing the merged raw events on demand.
elements.problem: Input devices can report far faster than the frame rate; delivering every raw event floods handlers, while coalescing delivers one event per frame with the raw history (e.g. getCoalescedEvents) available for precision uses like inking.
elements.named_in: Pointer Events Level 2 - W3C Recommendation (coalesced events / getCoalescedEvents)

elements.name: Signals and Slots
elements.what: A type-safe callback mechanism where objects declare signals they emit and slots (member functions) that can be connected to any compatible signal, with the framework routing emissions to all connected slots.
elements.problem: Raw function-pointer callbacks are type-unsafe and couple caller to callee; signals/slots decouple emitter from receivers with checked signatures and many-to-many connections. Qt's canonical realization of Observer; also Boost.Signals2, GTK signals.
elements.named_in: Signals & Slots - Qt Documentation - The Qt Company

elements.name: Hydration
elements.what: Attaches client-side behavior (event listeners, component state) to server-rendered static markup by re-running component logic and adopting the existing DOM instead of re-creating it.
elements.problem: Server-side rendering delivers fast first paint but inert markup; hydration makes it interactive without discarding the server's work, and mismatch detection guards divergence. Partial/lazy hydration and resumability (Qwik) are variants noted here.
elements.named_in: Server-Side Rendering (SSR) - Vue.js documentation (Client Hydration)
elements.borderline: Web-platform-specific rendering technique; passes the altitude test (implementable in one component, named, recurring) but domain-narrow.

elements.name: Update Batching
elements.what: Buffers multiple state mutations occurring in one synchronous turn and flushes their downstream effects (re-render, DOM patch) once, typically on the next microtask or tick, deduplicating redundant work.
elements.problem: Naively reacting to every individual state write causes repeated renders and observable intermediate states; queueing and deduplicating watchers per tick makes updates coalesce (React automatic batching, Vue's async update queue / nextTick).
elements.named_in: React documentation - Automatic Batching (React 18); Vue.js Guide - Reactivity in Depth (Async Update Queue)

parked_architecture.name: Model-View-Controller (MVC)
parked_architecture.why: Whole-app structural decomposition of responsibilities (Reenskaug/Smalltalk-80; POSA 1) - app-structure altitude, Phase 3.

parked_architecture.name: Model-View-Presenter (MVP)
parked_architecture.why: App-structure variant of MVC (Potel; Fowler's Passive View and Supervising Controller are its sub-variants) - Phase 3.

parked_architecture.name: Model-View-ViewModel (MVVM)
parked_architecture.why: App-structure pattern (Gossman, Microsoft WPF) built on data binding; the binding mechanism is cataloged as a design element, the structure parks here.

parked_architecture.name: Presentation-Abstraction-Control (PAC)
parked_architecture.why: POSA 1 architectural pattern - hierarchical agent decomposition of an interactive system, system-structure altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Presentation Model
parked_architecture.why: Fowler GUI-architecture pattern (2004) - app-structure separation predecessor of MVVM.

parked_architecture.name: Flux
parked_architecture.why: Facebook's application architecture for unidirectional data flow (dispatcher/store/view) - app-structure altitude; Redux/centralized-store is its best-known descendant.

parked_architecture.name: Elm Architecture
parked_architecture.why: aka Model-View-Update (MVU); whole-app structure (model/update/view triad) from the Elm guide - app-structure altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Unidirectional Data Flow
parked_architecture.why: App-wide data-flow discipline umbrella (Flux/Elm/MVI family) - a constraint on system structure, not an in-component mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Model-View-Intent (MVI)
parked_architecture.why: Reactive app-structure variant (cycle.js lineage) of unidirectional data flow - Phase 3 with the MV* family.

parked_architecture.name: Islands Architecture
parked_architecture.why: Page-level structure for partial hydration (Astro et al.); the hydration mechanism itself is cataloged as a design element.

excluded_notable.name: Event bubbling / capturing
excluded_notable.why: Raw DOM platform dispatch semantics (DOM spec feature), not a design element; event delegation - the mechanism built on it - is cataloged.

excluded_notable.name: Controlled / uncontrolled components
excluded_notable.why: React-framework-specific idiom for where form state lives; folded conceptually under data binding rather than cataloged.

excluded_notable.name: React Hooks
excluded_notable.why: Framework-proprietary API surface, not a cross-codebase mechanism name.

excluded_notable.name: Skeleton screens
excluded_notable.why: UX/perceived-performance presentation practice (Wroblewski) rather than an implementation mechanism.

notes: Coverage: charter's 10 named targets all resolved (data binding; virtual DOM+reconciliation as one element; signals spot-checked live on TC39 proposal; observables spot-checked on reactivex.io with backpressure noted as Reactive Streams territory shared with resilience scout; event delegation; immediate-mode GUI IN as borderline plus retained-mode counterpart; dirty rectangles with games-scout overlap; event loop carried with message-pump aka per charter, concurrency scout owns primary; undo/redo command stack decided IN as borderline composition, spot-checked on refactoring.guru; reactive programming decided IN as borderline umbrella with FRP split out as its own precisely-named element). Elm/Flux/MV*/PAC/Presentation Model all parked for Phase 3. Additions beyond charter list: dirty checking, list virtualization, optimistic UI, debounce/throttle (scheduling scout overlap), event coalescing, signals-and-slots, hydration, update batching. Deliberately skipped as other scouts' territory: double buffering and game loop (games), event queue (games/communication), Observer itself (oo-patterns), memoized selectors (caching). Thin spots: native/desktop toolkit vocabulary beyond Qt (e.g. Cocoa KVO folded away, Win32 owner-draw not cataloged), and accessibility-tree mechanisms - no established element-level names confirmed this session.
